prompt.context: Our client is Roadrunner Railways. They are a large railway company that ships freight throughout the United States. Roadrunner is facing declining profitability and the CEO has approached us for guidance.
prompt.question: What areas would you explore to identify reasons for the declining profits?

clarifying_info.q: What does the competitive landscape look like?
clarifying_info.a: It is an oligopoly with a few large firms. There is little product differentiation, price-sensitive business customers, price competition with economies of scale benefits, and substitutes such as trucks, boats, and planes.

clarifying_info.q: Has revenue or cost changed more significantly?
clarifying_info.a: Both revenue and cost factors are in scope — the client has not isolated a single driver yet.

exhibits.title: Cost Breakdown by Department — Roadrunner vs. Competitors
exhibits.shows: A table comparing Roadrunner's departmental costs in absolute dollars (millions) against three competitors (Speedy Gonzales, Coyote, Flash) expressed as a percentage of total cost.
exhibits.data: Roadrunner total cost $2,000M; Finance $140M; Operations $950M; Sales & Marketing $450M; HR $120M; IT $260M; Other $80M. Competitor % of total cost columns provided for all departments.

exhibits.title: Revenue Retention and Growth by Customer Segment — Outsource vs. In-House Scenarios
exhibits.shows: A table showing total revenue and number of accounts for Large, Medium, and Small segments, with two scenarios: (1) keeping sales and marketing outsourced and (2) moving it in-house. Each scenario provides expected account retention % and expected account growth % over one year.
exhibits.data: Large: $1,200M revenue, 40 accounts; Medium: $1,000M revenue, 50 accounts; Small: $550M revenue, 75 accounts. Scenario 1 (Outsource): Large 100% retention 10% growth, Medium 100% retention 8% growth, Small 100% retention 6% growth. Scenario 2 (In-House): Large 75% retention 8% growth, Medium 95% retention 20% growth, Small 100% retention 25% growth.

framework: Revenue: examine changes in customer demand, customers switching to other freight transport modes (trucks, shipping, air), competition offering better prices or contracts, new leaner entrants with lower legacy costs
Cost — Maintenance: spare parts, frequency of repairs
Cost — Labor: train crew, maintenance crew, office workers
Cost — Sales & Marketing: freight contracts require relationship management
Industry context: oligopoly, little product differentiation, price-sensitive customers, economies of scale, stable growth tied to economy, competition from trucks/boats/planes

questions.prompt: After showing Exhibit A, what areas would you explore based on the cost benchmarking data?
questions.guidance: Candidate should normalize Roadrunner's absolute costs to percentages and compare to the competitor average. Roadrunner's Sales & Marketing is 22.5% of total cost vs. competitor range of 10–15% — a clear outlier. Operations and IT are also worth noting but Sales & Marketing is the primary flag. Candidate should identify Sales & Marketing for deeper investigation and ask about its primary cost buckets: labor, advertising, and travel expenses.

math.setup: Convert Roadrunner departmental dollars to % of $2,000M total cost, then compare to competitor averages.
math.answer: Sales & Marketing at ~22.5% is roughly double the competitor average of ~12%, making it the primary area for investigation.

questions.prompt: Roadrunner's Sales & Marketing is currently outsourced to a firm with centers across the country. Roadrunner pays for allocated employees called Marketing Consultants. The following data was obtained: Outsource: 1,860 employees at $80K each; In-House (central location): 620 employees at $120K each. What can you infer from this data, and what would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare total cost of each option. In-house is significantly cheaper despite the higher per-employee cost because the headcount is dramatically lower (one-third). Candidate should also explain why in-house requires fewer employees: less turnover, greater specialization, proximity to other functions, better performance management. Recommendation: move Sales & Marketing in-house.

math.setup: Total cost = number of employees × cost per employee for each option.
math.answer: Moving in-house saves $74.4M annually (50% cost reduction) despite a 50% higher per-employee cost, because headcount drops by 67%.

questions.prompt: You've now dramatically rearranged the sales force. What are potential repercussions and additional factors to consider?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will brainstorm broadly and arrive at the critical point that centralized in-house reps can no longer visit clients on-site, which affects service quality and relationship depth — especially for the large segment. This sets up the revenue analysis in Exhibit B.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit B, calculate the change in revenue if Sales & Marketing is moved fully in-house.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute projected revenue for each segment under both scenarios and compare. Key insight: in-house improves Medium and Small segment growth but significantly hurts the Large segment due to retention drop from 100% to 75%. The overall net change in projected revenue is negative in the short term for in-house.

math.setup: For each segment: Projected Revenue = Total Revenue × Retention % × (1 + Growth %). Change in revenue = In-House projected − Outsource projected.
steps: Large — Outsource: 1,200 × 100% × 110% = 1,320M; In-House: 1,200 × 75% = 900M retained, 900 × 108% = 972M projected. Immediate change: −300M. Projected change: 972 − 1,320 = −348M
Medium — Outsource: 1,000 × 100% × 108% = 1,080M; In-House: 1,000 × 95% = 950M retained, 950 × 120% = 1,140M projected. Immediate change: −50M. Projected change: 1,140 − 1,080 = +60M
Small — Outsource: 550 × 100% × 106% = 583M; In-House: 550 × 100% = 550M retained, 550 × 125% = 688M projected. Immediate change: 0. Projected change: 688 − 583 = +105M
math.answer: Moving fully in-house results in an immediate revenue decline of $350M and a net projected revenue decline of $183M, driven almost entirely by Large segment losses.

questions.prompt: What are your general observations of the data in Exhibit B, and what are the implications?
questions.guidance: Strong candidate observes: (1) all segments decline immediately under in-house, (2) Medium and Small show higher growth in-house while Large shows lower growth. Root cause: outsourced Marketing Consultants focused on Large accounts (larger commissions), so switching in-house increases touch with Small/Medium but reduces coverage of Large. Implication: a hybrid approach — move Small and Medium in-house, keep Large outsourced.

brainstorming.prompt: You've decided to move Sales & Marketing in-house for small and medium segments. What factors need to be considered in executing this transition?

categories.name: Transition Costs
ideas: Hiring and onboarding new in-house employees
Obtaining and fitting out office space
Training on Roadrunner products and systems
Contract breakage fees with the outsourcing firm

categories.name: Relationship Continuity
ideas: Impact on relationships the Marketing Consultants had built
Customers accustomed to in-person visits may be dissatisfied with phone-only contact
Loss of on-site customer insights that cannot be gathered remotely
Fewer employees may mean fewer client touchpoints

categories.name: Operational Integration
ideas: Ability to smoothly transition client relationships
Proximity of sales staff to operations and product teams
Performance management systems for in-house reps
Potential integration issues with internal IT/CRM systems

categories.name: Workforce Considerations
ideas: Availability of qualified local labor pool

recommendation: Roadrunner should reorganize its Sales & Marketing department as the primary lever to restore profitability
Move Sales & Marketing in-house for Small and Medium customer segments to reduce costs and capture higher growth
Keep the Large segment outsourced to preserve critical account relationships and retention rates
This hybrid approach captures $74.4M in labor cost savings on the in-house portion while protecting the largest revenue source
risks: Revenue loss during transition period as client relationships are handed over
Large segment retention could still erode if outsourced team performance declines
In-house headcount may be insufficient to maintain adequate client touchpoints
Integration and setup costs could offset near-term savings
next_steps: Quantify transition costs: hiring, office space, IT, training, contract breakage fees
Assess local labor pool availability and compensation benchmarks
Develop a phased transition plan to minimize service disruption
Model the net P&L impact combining cost savings minus transition costs minus projected revenue loss
Monitor Large segment account health closely under continued outsourcing
